Task 4: SMS Spam Detection (Spam vs Ham Classifier)¶

Author: Zareen Sabri | Track: Data Science | Internship: Oasis Infobyte (OIBSIP)

In this notebook I build a classifier that decides whether a text message is spam or ham (a normal message). I used the SMS Spam Collection dataset, which has 5,572 labelled messages.

Note on the dataset: Task 4 in the brief is called "Email Spam Detection", but its own sourcing guideline points to the SMS Spam Collection dataset (Kaggle / UCI). So the data here is SMS text messages, not emails. The method (text cleaning, TF-IDF, Naive Bayes / SVM) is exactly the same for emails, but the results should be treated as results for SMS data. To run it on emails, only the data loading cell needs to change.

The steps are: clean the text, turn it into numbers with TF-IDF, train a few models and compare them.

1. Imports¶

In [1]:

About 86.6% of the messages are ham and only 13.4% are spam, so the data is imbalanced. A model that predicted "ham" every time would get around 87% accuracy and catch no spam at all. Because of this I will look at precision, recall and F1 for the spam class and not just accuracy.

There are also 403 duplicate messages. I kept them since they are probably real repeated messages (like "Ok" or spam templates).

4. Text preprocessing¶

Models can't use raw text so I clean it first:

  1. make everything lowercase
  2. remove numbers and punctuation
  3. remove stopwords (common words like "the" and "is")
  4. stemming, which cuts words down to their root (for example "winning" becomes "win")

stemmer = PorterStemmer()

def clean_text(text):
    text = text.lower()                                           # 1. lowercase
    text = re.sub(r"\d+", " ", text)                              #    drop digits
    text = text.translate(str.maketrans("", "", string.punctuation))  # 2. punctuation
    tokens = [w for w in text.split() if w not in stop_words]     # 3. stopwords
    tokens = [stemmer.stem(w) for w in tokens]                    # 4. stemming
    return " ".join(tokens)

# test the cleaning on one message

5. TF-IDF¶

TF-IDF stands for term frequency - inverse document frequency. It gives each word a score for each message.

  • Term frequency (TF) is how often the word shows up in that message.
  • Inverse document frequency (IDF) is lower for words that appear in lots of messages and higher for rare words.

Multiplying them gives a high score to words that are common in one message but rare overall. That way very common words don't dominate the way they would with a simple word count. I also included word pairs (bigrams) like "call now" and ignored words that appear in fewer than 2 messages.

6. Train/test split¶

In [7]:
X_train_txt, X_test_txt, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    df["clean"], df["label_num"],
    test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=df["label_num"]   # stratify keeps the same spam ratio in both sets
)
print("Train:", len(X_train_txt), "| Test:", len(X_test_txt))
print("Spam share in train: %.1f%% | in test: %.1f%%" % (y_train.mean()*100, y_test.mean()*100))

# fit tfidf on the training data only
tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2)
X_train = tfidf.fit_transform(X_train_txt)
X_test = tfidf.transform(X_test_txt)
print("Number of TF-IDF features:", X_train.shape[1])

Train: 4457 | Test: 1115
Spam share in train: 13.4% | in test: 13.4%
Number of TF-IDF features: 7183

7. Training the models¶

I trained three models: Multinomial Naive Bayes (the standard choice for text), Logistic Regression and a Linear SVM. For the last two I used class_weight="balanced" because of the imbalance.

In [8]:
models = {
    "Multinomial Naive Bayes": MultinomialNB(alpha=0.1),
    "Logistic Regression":     LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced"),
    "Linear SVM":              LinearSVC(class_weight="balanced"),
}

preds = {}
for name, m in models.items():
    m.fit(X_train, y_train)
    preds[name] = m.predict(X_test)
print("Models trained")

Models trained

9. Why is recall important for spam detection?¶

Recall is the share of all real spam messages that the model catches: TP / (TP + FN).

If recall is low, a lot of spam gets through to the inbox. Some of those messages are scams or phishing links, so missing them can cause real harm.

But recall is not the only thing to look at. If the model marked everything as spam it would have 100% recall and be useless, because real messages would end up in the spam folder too. That is what precision measures. F1 combines both. In practice a good filter needs high recall and high precision, and wrongly blocking a real message is also a serious problem (for example a bank code or a job offer).

11. Testing on new messages¶

In [14]:
best = models["Linear SVM"]   # best model from the comparison

def predict_message(msg, model=best):
    vec = tfidf.transform([clean_text(msg)])
    return "SPAM" if model.predict(vec)[0] == 1 else "HAM"

tests = [
    "Congratulations! You've won a free iPhone. Click here to claim your prize now!",
    "Hey, are we still meeting for lunch at 1?",
    "URGENT: your account has been suspended. Call 0800 123 456 to verify immediately.",
    "Can you pick up some milk on your way home?",
    "WINNER!! You have been selected for a 500 cash reward. Text CLAIM to 80082",
]
for t in tests:
    print(f"{predict_message(t):10s} | {t}")

12. Conclusion¶

Model Accuracy Precision Recall F1
Naive Bayes 0.979 0.985 0.859 0.918
Logistic Regression 0.977 0.907 0.919 0.913
Linear SVM 0.983 0.951 0.919 0.935

(precision, recall and F1 are for the spam class)

The Linear SVM is the best model. It has the highest accuracy and F1, and its recall is tied with Logistic Regression. It caught about 137 of the 149 spam messages in the test set.

Naive Bayes had the best precision (almost everything it called spam really was spam) but the lowest recall, so about 21 spam messages got through. Logistic Regression had the same recall as the SVM but wrongly flagged more real messages, which lowered its precision.

Some limits to keep in mind. The test set only has 149 spam messages, so the gap between Logistic Regression and the SVM is small. The data is also older SMS data with a lot of slang, so a model like this would need to be retrained before being used on modern emails.

Next steps could be tuning the model settings with cross-validation and adding message length as a feature.
